question: In the §03 walkthrough the descent to `id = 424242` reads the root, internal page 74, leaf 3151, then heap page 8191 — 3 index pages + 1 heap page, of which only one or two are real I/O because the ~8 pages above the leaves stay resident. The fixture holds 1,000,000 rows; capacity planning now projects 10,000,000. A colleague budgets roughly ten times the per-lookup page reads and proposes partitioning the table to keep lookups cheap. Reading the same arithmetic the walkthrough used, what actually happens to that descent at 10M rows?
choices: Per-lookup cost tracks the row count, because the leaf level is what a descent ultimately walks: ten times the rows means ten times the leaf pages under the same separators, so the final step becomes a multi-page scan rather than a single read. Partitioning is the standard fix precisely because it caps the size of any one index

Depth stays at 3, but the constant factor moves with the row count: each leaf page must now hold ten times the entries, so the binary search inside leaf 3151 grows from roughly nine comparisons to ninety and the leaf read spans several pages

Each level multiplies capacity by the fan-out — ~370 entries per page in this fixture — so depth 3 covers ~370³ ≈ 50M rows. At 10M the leaf level grows from ~2,700 to ~27,000 pages and the internal level from ~7 to ~73, yet a lookup still reads 3 index pages + 1 heap page, and the root plus internal level is still well under a megabyte that stays in shared buffers. The steady-state one-or-two real reads is unchanged; a fourth level appears only past ~50M rows, and costs one more page that is also almost always cached

Depth is driven by the number of distinct keys the tree must separate, so a dense sequential `bigint` key builds a much taller tree than a sparse one: at 10M sequential ids `users_pkey` reaches depth 5 or 6. For pure equality lookups like this one the right move is a hash index, whose lookup is depth-independent
explanation: The walkthrough's numbers are not decoration — they are the derivation of the depth. A leaf page holds ~370 `(key, TID)` entries, so 1M rows need ~2,700 leaf pages; ~2,700 downlinks need ~7 internal pages; 7 fit in one root. That is depth 3, and the same multiplication says depth 3 stretches to ~370³ ≈ 50M rows before a fourth level is forced. Growing 10× therefore changes the *width* of the tree (27,000 leaves, 73 internal pages) and not the *height*, which is the whole point of a B-tree: search cost is logarithmic in a base of several hundred, so it moves in steps of one page read per two-orders-of-magnitude of growth. The second half of the reasoning matters as much as the first: the tree's non-leaf levels stay tiny in absolute terms (74 pages ≈ 600 KB at 10M rows), so they remain buffer-resident and steps 1–2 remain free, leaving the leaf and the heap page as the only candidates for real I/O — exactly the steady state the walkthrough reports today. Partitioning may still be justified by vacuum windows, retention, or bulk drops, but 'lookups will get expensive' is not the reason, and a partitioned lookup that must also identify the partition is not automatically cheaper. The distractors each break the arithmetic in a different place: leaves multiply but a descent reads exactly one of them, since the separators name a single downlink per level; leaf pages are 8 KB and cannot absorb ten times the entries — overflow is what triggers the split of §06, not a denser page; and depth follows entry count through fan-out regardless of whether keys are dense or sparse, while a hash index would buy an O(1) lookup only by giving up ranges and ordering entirely for a plan that is already one or two page reads.

question: In the §06 trace, W splits leaf 3151 at t3 and releases its locks immediately, but only posts the separator 424100 and the downlink to page 9001 into parent 74 at t4. Consider a third session S that begins its descent for `id = 425500` inside that window: it read-locks parent 74 after t3 but before t4, so the parent still tells it `(421000, 427000] → leaf 3151`. What does S do, and what does its behaviour say about the t4 step?
choices: S is not in that window at all: the split takes an exclusive lock on parent 74 from the moment it decides to split until the separator is posted, so any descent arriving between t3 and t4 waits. That interval is short, but it is exactly why a split is described as a two-page operation rather than a one-page one

S reads a parent that no longer describes the tree, detects the mismatch by comparing parent 74's page LSN against the value it read before locking, and restarts its descent from the root. The restart is harmless but it is why a split must post to the parent promptly — a slow t4 turns into a retry storm at the top of the tree

S lands on 3151 just as R did, finds `425500 > high key 424100`, and follows the right-link to 9001 — the same move-right recovery, reached from a stale downlink rather than from a read that was already in flight. A downlink is therefore only a hint whose sole obligation is never to point past the key being searched; it is allowed to lag, which is precisely why t4 can be a separate, unlocked, deferrable step and why the split at t3 could drop its locks without waiting for it

S gets a wrong answer, and that is the known limit of the trace: move-right rescues only readers like R, which read the parent before the split and are therefore still on the pre-split path. A session that reads the parent after the split has no in-flight state to repair, so PostgreSQL performs the parent insert inside the same critical section as the split, making the t3/t4 split in the trace a simplification
explanation: The move-right recovery is not a special case for readers caught mid-operation — it is the tree's general rule for arriving at a page whose coverage has shrunk, and it makes no distinction between 'I read the parent before the split' and 'I read a parent that had not been updated yet'. S locks 3151, compares its key against the page's high key, sees 425500 exceed 424100, and walks the right-link to 9001, where the high key 427000 covers it. Both cases are the same check against the same field. What this buys is the property the whole design rests on: because a stale downlink is still a *safe* downlink — it can only land a searcher too far left, never past the key — the parent insert is not part of the split's critical section. W can therefore split, release, and post afterwards, and readers never wait on the multi-page operation as a whole. Making t4 atomic with t3 would reintroduce exactly the coupling the structure exists to avoid, and would put the contention back at the internal levels, which every descent passes through. The distractors each restore a cost the design removes: locking parent 74 across the split serialises descents through that subtree for the duration; an LSN check plus a restart from the root discards the cheap local repair in favour of re-walking levels that were already correct; and the claim that S gets a wrong answer inverts the guarantee — a searcher that finds its key above the high key knows the page moved and knows where it went, which is the same information R used at t4.

question: At t3 of the §07 trace, `SELECT ctid, xmin, xmax …` inside session A shows v1 at `(7,2)` carrying `xmax = 951` from a transaction that has already committed, while every other session is reading v2 at `(7,5)`. An engineer watching the table bloat runs `VACUUM users` at exactly this moment, expecting to reclaim v1 along with the index entries pointing at `(7,2)`. What does the vacuum accomplish for this row, and why?
choices: Nothing for this row. `xmax = 951` is committed, but A's snapshot was frozen at t1 and still resolves v1 as visible, so v1 is not dead *to everyone*; vacuum computes the oldest snapshot in the cluster and leaves any version that snapshot could see, along with both index entries pointing at `(7,2)`. Reclaim becomes possible only once A ends — which is the real cost of a long-running transaction: it pins versions everywhere, not just in the rows it read

It reclaims v1 and both index entries. The tuple is dead because 951 committed and A holds no lock on it; A's next `SELECT` at t3 is then served from v2, which is the well-known way a `REPEATABLE READ` snapshot can shift under an aggressive vacuum

It reclaims v1 in the heap but leaves both index entries behind. VACUUM removes index entries only on a subsequent pass, after the transactions that could still see the version have ended, so the entries survive as pointers to a freed line pointer until the next cycle collects them

Nothing for this row, but for a different reason: A's `SELECT` at t1 took a row-level lock on `(7,2)` that it holds for the length of the transaction, and vacuum skips locked tuples and retries them on a later run. Without that lock the version would be reclaimed here, since 951 committed before the vacuum started
explanation: The trace makes visibility a function of (version header, snapshot), and cleanup inherits that arithmetic: a version is removable only when *no* snapshot in the cluster can resolve it as visible. A's frozen snapshot excludes 951, so for A the deletion has not happened, and vacuum — which works from the oldest snapshot still in play — must leave v1 in the heap and its entries in both indexes. This is why an idle-in-transaction session is a cluster-wide problem rather than a per-row one: the horizon it holds back blocks pruning and vacuuming for every table, including ones it never touched, and the visible symptom is bloat with a vacuum that appears to run and reclaim nothing. The lever is on the transaction, not the vacuum. The distractors each attack a different link in the chain: reclaiming v1 while A can see it would make `REPEATABLE READ` unable to keep its promise, which is the one thing the isolation level is for, so 'the snapshot shifts under vacuum' describes a bug rather than a behaviour. Freeing the heap tuple before deleting the index entries inverts the §09 ordering, and inverts it in the dangerous direction — a live index entry pointing at a freed line pointer could be handed a *different* row once that slot is reused, which is exactly why vacuum deletes index entries first and frees the line pointer last. And a plain `SELECT` under `REPEATABLE READ` takes no row-level lock; if lock-holding were the mechanism, a snapshot would only protect the rows it had already read, whereas the actual rule protects everything the snapshot could still go on to read.

question: In the §09 afterlife, act 2's `SELECT … WHERE id = 777` pays a wasted heap fetch and flips `LP_DEAD` on the entry in `users_pkey`, and act 3's repeat of it skips the heap entirely. Still before `VACUUM`, a different query arrives for the same dead row through the other index: `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = …`, served by `users_email_key`. What does that scan do, and what does the asymmetry actually cost?
choices: It skips the heap as well. `LP_DEAD` marks the state of the heap line pointer at `(12,3)`, so once any scan has established that the tuple is dead, every index entry that points at that TID observes the same fact — the asymmetry in the table is about which scan *paid* for the discovery, not about who benefits from it

It descends `users_email_key`, finds the entry unmarked, fetches heap page 12, finds the tuple dead to everyone, returns 0 rows — and sets `LP_DEAD` on its own leaf entry on the way out. Hints are per-index and earned by the scan that pays for them, so the asymmetry costs exactly one wasted heap fetch per index per dead entry, once. Nothing is actually removed from either index or the heap until act 4

It pays the fetch and returns 0 rows, but cannot set the hint: `LP_DEAD` is only ever set by a scan on the index backing the table's primary key, because only there is the TID reachable by a unique entry, so `users_email_key` re-pays the wasted fetch on every execution until `VACUUM` deletes the entry

The choice of index is irrelevant here, because both entries are already gone: committing the `DELETE` in act 1 removes the row's index entries synchronously, and what `VACUUM` adds at act 4 is freeing the heap line pointer so the slot becomes reusable
explanation: The hint is a property of the index entry, not of the heap tuple: setting `LP_DEAD` on the pkey entry records 'this entry's TID is dead, do not bother fetching it', and that note lives in the leaf page of `users_pkey`. `users_email_key` has its own leaf entry pointing at the same `(12,3)` and no note on it, so the first scan through it repeats the whole discovery — descend, fetch page 12, resolve the tuple as dead to everyone, return nothing — and then earns its own hint. The cost is therefore bounded and self-limiting: one wasted fetch per index per dead entry, after which that index skips too. The rest of the table's ledger holds throughout: the deletion is still purely a stamped `xmax` plus two live index entries, and only act 4's `VACUUM` — dead-TID list, delete from `users_pkey`, delete from `users_email_key`, *then* free line pointer `lp3` — removes anything. The distractors each move the hint to the wrong place: making `LP_DEAD` a property of the heap TID would require an index scan to read the heap page to learn that it need not read the heap page, which defeats the optimisation; restricting hint-setting to the primary key index has no basis in the mechanism and would make every secondary index re-pay forever, turning a one-off cost into a standing one; and having `DELETE` remove index entries synchronously would contradict act 1's whole point — a `DELETE` that is not yet dead to every snapshot must leave every version reachable, which is precisely why the index cleanup is deferred to `VACUUM` and why the corpse is held by three structures at once between acts 1 and 4.

question: In §10, a freshly vacuumed table gives `Heap Fetches: 0`, then a single-row `UPDATE users SET last_login = now() WHERE id = 100050` makes the same `id BETWEEN 100000 AND 100100` index-only scan report `Heap Fetches: 61`. A colleague calls the number a misreading: one row was modified, so at most one row's visibility is in question and the count should be 1. Trace where 61 comes from.
choices: The count is right and the reasoning is nearly right — it is just off by one page. The `UPDATE` cleared the bit on the page holding the old version *and* on the page receiving the new one, so 61 is the combined row count of those two pages; had `fillfactor` left room for a HOT update, the new version would have stayed on the same page and the scan would still report 0

61 counts index entries re-read, not heap trips. The non-HOT `UPDATE` inserted a second `users_pkey` entry for id 100050, and `Heap Fetches` reports the leaf entries an index-only scan must re-examine when the leaf changes underneath the range it is walking

The visibility map does track individual rows, but it is maintained lazily: the `UPDATE` queued the rows physically adjacent to the modified one for re-verification, and 61 is the size of that queue. The following `VACUUM` drains it, which is why the third `EXPLAIN` returns to 0

The scan checks visibility per TID, but the visibility map answers per heap *page*: the `UPDATE` cleared the all-visible bit of page 1667, and because the rows were loaded in `id` order, ~61 of the 101 ids in the range live on that page. The bit vouches for every tuple on a page or for none, so all 61 fall back to a heap fetch plus a snapshot check — including the 60 that were never touched. The unit of the optimisation is the page, so one write's blast radius is every row that shares its page
explanation: The whole reason an index-only scan is viable is that visibility was made a page-level question: one bit per heap page, small enough to stay cached, standing in for the per-tuple headers the index cannot see. That coarseness is the source of both the speed and this number. A write clears the bit for the page, not for the row, so the scan loses its shortcut for every one of the ~61 range members that happen to sit on page 1667 — an amplification factor set by how many of the scanned rows share a page, which here is high precisely because the rows were loaded in `id` order and the scan walks a contiguous `id` range. The practical reading is that `Heap Fetches` measures vacuum debt in units of pages touched by writes, that a clustered load pattern makes each write more expensive for range scans rather than less, and that the metric is meaningful only against a table with a realistic write history. The distractors each substitute a mechanism from a neighbouring section: HOT decides whether a version stays on its page and whether indexes must be touched, but it does not preserve the all-visible bit — any write to the page clears it, so a HOT update would also have produced a non-zero count, and `fillfactor` cannot buy back a 0. `Heap Fetches` counts exactly what it says, heap trips, not leaf re-reads; the scan's leaf walk is reported through buffer counts instead. And there is no per-row visibility state anywhere for a queue to hold — if there were, an index-only scan could consult it directly and the whole page-granularity trade-off, along with this jump from 0 to 61, would not exist.
